issues.legal_issue: A notice requirement for release of a tenanted building is satisfied when the law does not prescribe a mode of service and the evidence, considered with surrounding circumstances, establishes that the tenant received notice.
material_facts: A landlord sought release of a shop for personal business after purchasing it while it was occupied by a tenant.
The landlord produced a photocopy of a postal certificate receipt with an affidavit stating that notice had been sent.
The tenant admitted the landlord-tenant relationship and later applied to deposit rent in court after the notice was sent.
The authorities considered the receipt together with the tenant’s conduct and other circumstances and found that notice had been given and received at least six months before the release application.
The High Court rejected service on the ground that service could not be presumed from a postal certificate.
issues.conclusion: The notice requirement was satisfied; the finding of service was justified because it rested on the receipt, affidavit, and surrounding circumstances, not solely on a presumption from the postal certificate.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires notice but prescribes no particular mode, so notice may be oral or written and need not be sent by registered post. Section 34(1)(b) permits evidence on affidavit before the prescribed authority. Whether a postal-certificate notice establishes service depends on the facts: Sumitra Devi v. Sampuran Singh and Ranju v. Rekha Ghosh support service where the circumstances justify it; V.S. Krishnan v. Westfort Hi-Tech Hospitals recognizes the relevance of evidence that notices were sent and the addressee’s opportunity to rebut; Shiv Kumar v. State of Haryana is distinguishable because it concerned reliance on postal-certificate service alone and a prescribed mode of service.

rule.if: release_application_for_bona_fide_use and notice_mode_not_prescribed and postal_receipt_supported_by_affidavit and surrounding_circumstances_indicate_notice_received

predicates.release_application_for_bona_fide_use: A landlord applied to recover an occupied building for bona fide use by the landlord or a qualifying beneficiary.
predicates.notice_mode_not_prescribed: The governing notice requirement did not specify a particular method of giving notice.
predicates.postal_receipt_supported_by_affidavit: The landlord submitted a postal certificate receipt with an affidavit supporting the sending of notice.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_indicate_notic: The tenant’s conduct and other circumstances supported the finding that the tenant had notice.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks release for bona fide use, the law prescribes no notice method, and an affidavit-supported postal receipt is reinforced by circumstances indicating receipt, the notice requirement is satisfied.

issues.legal_issue: A writ court should not unsettle concurrent factual findings on service of notice when those findings rest on evidence and relevant circumstances rather than solely on a presumption from a postal receipt.
material_facts: The prescribed authority found that the tenant had received notice after considering the postal receipt, affidavit, the tenant’s admission of the landlord-tenant relationship, the tenant’s later rent-deposit application, and other circumstances.
The appellate authority affirmed that finding.
The High Court set aside the finding on the view that service could not be presumed from a postal certificate.
The Supreme Court concluded that the finding was not based merely on such a presumption.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought not to have set aside the supported concurrent finding that notice was served.
issues.legal_principle: A factual finding reached on valid reasons and supported by evidence and surrounding circumstances should not be unsettled in writ review merely because the notice was sent under a postal certificate. The court distinguished cases concerning criminal proceedings, matrimonial documents not supported by an affidavit, and service under rules prescribing a specific method; it applied the approach in Sumitra Devi v. Sampuran Singh, Ranju v. Rekha Ghosh, and V.S. Krishnan v. Westfort Hi-Tech Hospitals concerning fact-dependent proof of service.

predicates.writ_review_of_release_order: A writ court reviewed an order allowing an application to release a tenanted building.
predicates.two_lower_authorities_made_same_factual_: The first-instance authority and the appellate authority reached the same factual finding.
predicates.finding_supported_by_evidence_and_circum: The authorities relied on evidence and surrounding circumstances in reaching that finding.
predicates.finding_not_based_only_on_postal_receipt: The authorities did not rely solely on the fact that a notice had been sent under a postal certificate.

issues.definition: In writ review of a release order, when both lower authorities reach the same factual finding on evidence and circumstances rather than on a postal receipt alone, the writ court should not set that finding aside.

issues.legal_issue: A supported finding that the landlord would suffer greater comparative hardship should stand when the writ court has not specifically considered or categorically displaced it.
material_facts: The prescribed authority and appellate authority found that the landlord’s hardship would be greater than the tenant’s and allowed release.
The prescribed authority noted that the landlord had no shop for the intended business and that there was no evidence that the tenant had tried to find alternative accommodation.
The High Court did not specifically consider or categorically set aside the comparative-hardship finding.
issues.conclusion: The comparative-hardship finding did not warrant interference and remained effective.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding an application for release under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the factual assessment of comparative hardship by the prescribed and appellate authorities should not be disturbed where the reviewing court has not specifically considered or categorically displaced that finding. No earlier case was cited for this point.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_review_of_release_order: An appeal challenged a writ judgment reviewing an order on an application to release a tenanted building.
predicates.lower_authorities_found_landlord_hardshi: The first-instance and appellate authorities found that the landlord would suffer greater hardship than the tenant.
predicates.writ_court_did_not_categorically_displac: The writ court did not specifically consider or categorically overturn the comparative-hardship finding.

issues.definition: When an appeal arises from writ review of a release order, the lower authorities found greater hardship to the landlord, and the writ court did not categorically displace that finding, the comparative-hardship finding stands.
